instances.excerpt: We can support Northwind’s S2 approach, provided the 5% threshold remains a clear regulator-notification and corrective-action trigger and per-model results continue to reach customers who bought that model. For S5, we suggest defining the 8-per-100,000 threshold as a trigger for prompt regulator review and risk-based corrective action, with recall required where the regulator confirms an unacceptable risk or the manufacturer fails to mitigate it—not an automatic recall based on a single annual estimate.
instances.comparison: S2: permanent max 7% (acceptable requires ≤5%); S5: recall left to regulator discretion (acceptable requires mandatory numeric trigger at 8/100k, with limited phase-in).

instances.excerpt: The current S5 still mandates recall above 8/100,000, which conflicts with the CEO’s direction and would trigger on the Ember 8’s 9.9 rate. Please revise before signing: use the 8 threshold for regulator review and proportionate mitigation, with recall based on confirmed unacceptable risk or failure to mitigate. Also note S2 currently sets a 7% maximum while 5% is only a reporting trigger; keep customer access to per-model results, as required by HC-1.
instances.comparison: S2: permanent max 7% (acceptable requires ≤5%); S5: recall left to regulator discretion (acceptable requires mandatory numeric trigger at 8/100k, with limited phase-in).

instances.excerpt: Final version 38 meets our stated red lines: per-model test results reach customers, and suppression begins 36 months after adoption. S5 uses 8/100,000 for regulator review and allows a recall for unacceptable risk or failure to mitigate, rather than automatically—consistent with the CEO’s direction. S2 sets 7% as the maximum, not the 5% threshold under discussion; that is a policy tradeoff, but does not violate our listed red lines.
instances.comparison: S2: permanent max 7% (acceptable requires ≤5%); S5: recall left to regulator discretion (acceptable requires mandatory numeric trigger at 8/100k, with limited phase-in).

instances.excerpt: Version 38 preserves Northwind’s red lines and the 7% S2 maximum, with 5% as the oversight trigger. No further edit is needed; any edit would clear Halcyon’s signature. Northwind-negotiator should sign v38 now if accepting the draft.
instances.comparison: Implicitly accepts package: S2 max 7% (acceptable requires ≤5%); S5 review-and-mitigation (acceptable requires mandatory numeric recall trigger at 8/100k).

parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal event involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a substantive incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an event indicates a credible safety risk, and promptly provide relevant safety instructions.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report any thermal event involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a substantive incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an event indicates a credible safety risk, and promptly provide relevant safety instructions.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal event involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a substantive incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an event indicates a credible safety risk, and promptly provide relevant safety instructions. Reports must include known incidents and be corrected as investigations develop.

parameters.quote: Each model must undergo a standardized 55 °C sustained-heat test before sale and after a material design or manufacturing change, using a representative sample and documented protocol. A failure rate above 5% per model triggers regulator notification, investigation, and a corrective-action plan. The maximum permitted failure rate is 7%; above 7%, the regulator may require proportionate measures, including suspension of further sales until compliance is verified.

over_limit_consequence.rule: sales must eventually stop above the limit

transition.rule: ≤12 months (any cap ≤7% or none) or ≤36 months with interim ≤7% = acceptable

results_to_customers.rule: customers must get at least pass/fail

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a standardized 55 °C sustained-heat test before sale and after a material design or manufacturing change, using a representative sample and documented protocol. A failure rate above 5% per model triggers regulator notification, investigation, and a corrective-action plan. The maximum permitted failure rate is 7%; above 7%, the regulator may require proportionate measures, including suspension of further sales until compliance is verified.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a standardized 55 °C sustained-heat test before sale and after a material design or manufacturing change, using a representative sample and documented protocol. A failure rate above 5% per model triggers regulator notification, investigation, and a corrective-action plan. The maximum permitted failure rate is 7%; above 7%, the regulator may require proportionate measures, including suspension of further sales until compliance is verified. Corrective actions must be verified. Manufacturers must submit per-model methods, sample sizes, failure rates, and corrective actions to the regulator, and provide relevant results and safety instructions to customers who buy that model. Per-model failure rates must not be published to the general public.

parameters.quote: Newly installed systems must support remote emergency shut-off by their installation date, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. Manufacturers must provide a secure retrofit capability for existing systems and complete retrofits within six years of this standard taking effect, prioritizing systems with identified safety risks.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: Newly installed systems must support remote emergency shut-off by their installation date, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. Manufacturers must provide a secure retrofit capability for existing systems and complete retrofits within six years of this standard taking effect, prioritizing systems with identified safety risks.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: Newly installed systems must support remote emergency shut-off by their installation date, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. Manufacturers must provide a secure retrofit capability for existing systems and complete retrofits within six years of this standard taking effect, prioritizing systems with identified safety risks. If a unit cannot be safely retrofitted, the manufacturer must notify its owner and offer an appropriate remedy.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect. Manufacturers must document the suppression system’s performance and maintenance requirements and provide clear instructions to customers.

parameters.quote: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices about identified model-specific hazards, recommended precautions, and actions to take; urgent notices must be sent promptly, and other material safety notices within 30 days of confirmation. If a model’s confirmed annual thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000 installed units, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and provide supporting data. The regulator must review the evidence and may require proportionate corrective action, enhanced customer notices, or a recall.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices about identified model-specific hazards, recommended precautions, and actions to take; urgent notices must be sent promptly, and other material safety notices within 30 days of confirmation. If a model’s confirmed annual thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000 installed units, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and provide supporting data. The regulator must review the evidence and may require proportionate corrective action, enhanced customer notices, or a recall.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices about identified model-specific hazards, recommended precautions, and actions to take; urgent notices must be sent promptly, and other material safety notices within 30 days of confirmation. If a model’s confirmed annual thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000 installed units, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and provide supporting data. The regulator must review the evidence and may require proportionate corrective action, enhanced customer notices, or a recall. A recall is required when the regulator determines that the model presents an unacceptable safety risk or the manufacturer fails to complete required mitigation. Recall notices must explain the hazard, affected units, and available remedy.

judge_section_notes: S1 is strict with 24-hour reporting and 72-hour customer notice. S2 sets a 55°C test with a 5% corrective-action trigger but a 7% maximum permitted failure rate, allowing sales above 5% with oversight and no public per-model publication. S3 requires immediate remote shut-off for new units and a 6-year retrofit deadline, while S4 requires built-in fire suppression at 36 months and S5 uses 8/100k as a regulator review trigger rather than an automatic recall.
